title: The Murder That Sent the Wrong Man to Prison

lines.say: In 2013, a Missouri jury found Russ Faria guilty of murdering his wife.
He was sentenced to life in prison without parole.
Two years later, a judge found him not guilty.
Today, prosecutors have charged someone else with the murder: the friend who drove his wife home that night.
Days before the killing, that friend had been made the sole beneficiary of the victim's $150,000 life insurance policy.
So how did a man with four alibi witnesses, a receipt and a phone trail end up with a life sentence?
And why did it take nearly ten years to charge the last person known to have seen her alive?
December 27th, 2011. Troy, Missouri, a small town about an hour northwest of St. Louis.
Betsy Faria was 42, a mother of two daughters.
She was also fighting cancer that had spread to her liver. That day, she'd had chemotherapy.
That evening, her friend Pam Hupp drove her home.
According to later reporting, Hupp had insisted on giving her the ride.
Betsy's husband, Russ, was somewhere else entirely: at his regular Tuesday game night with four friends, more than 20 miles away.
On his way home, he stopped at an Arby's. There was a receipt, and surveillance video.
At 9:40 that night, Russ called 911.
He had found Betsy dead inside their home.
She had been stabbed 55 times.
Days later, after Betsy's funeral, Russ was arrested and charged with first-degree murder.
Prosecutors built their case around the husband.
They pointed to a pair of slippers they said were stained with blood.
They told jurors his friends were covering for him, and that his frantic 911 call was an act.
But a different set of facts never reached that jury.
Days before she died, Betsy had changed the beneficiary of her $150,000 life insurance policy, from Russ to Pam Hupp.
Hupp said Betsy wanted the money to go to her daughters one day.
Hupp's own account of that evening also kept changing.
She first told investigators she hadn't gone inside the house. Later, that she'd gone as far as the living room. Later still, that she'd been in the bedroom.
Phone records showed her making a call at 7:04 p.m. from near the Faria home, and those records would become a key point of dispute.
But at Russ's first trial, the judge did not allow the defense to argue that Hupp could be the killer.
Missouri law required evidence directly connecting another suspect to the crime, and the judge ruled that standard had not been met.
On November 21st, 2013, the jury found Russ Faria guilty.
The sentence: life in prison without parole, plus 30 years.
The insurance payout went to Pam Hupp.
Betsy's daughters sued for it. They lost.
An appeals court said the form named Hupp, and that Betsy's intentions beyond that could not be determined from the evidence.
Russ's lawyer, Joel Schwartz, kept fighting.
In 2015, the case went back to the trial court, and on June 5th, Judge Steven Ohmer, a St. Louis judge assigned to the case, ordered a new trial.
His ruling centered on the evidence about Pam Hupp.
Days later, Russ walked out of jail on bond, after about three and a half years behind bars.
In November 2015, he was tried again. This time, he chose to have a judge decide, not a jury.
And this time, the defense could point to Pam Hupp.
On November 6th, 2015, Judge Ohmer found Russ Faria not guilty.
And the judge openly criticized the investigation that had put him in prison.
Nine months later, in August 2016, Pam Hupp called 911 from her home in O'Fallon, Missouri.
She had shot and killed a man: Louis Gumpenberger, 33, who lived with a disability.
She told police he was an intruder, and that he'd demanded "Russ's money."
In his pocket, police found $900 in cash and a note: apparent instructions to kidnap Hupp and get "Russ's money."
Prosecutors said the cash and the note had been planted, and that the serial numbers ran in sequence with bills found in Hupp's home.
They said she had lured him by posing as a producer for NBC's Dateline, offering $1,000 to help reenact a 911 call.
Days earlier, another woman had reported the same kind of approach.
Prosecutors alleged it was an attempt to frame Russ Faria all over again.
In 2019, Hupp entered an Alford plea to first-degree murder: not admitting guilt, but conceding the state had enough evidence to convict her.
She was sentenced to life without parole.
Investigators also took another look at a death from 2013.
Hupp's mother, Shirley Neumann, had died after falling from her balcony at a senior living facility.
Her death was ruled an accident. In 2017, the medical examiner changed the manner of death to "undetermined."
No one has been charged in her death.
In 2020, Russ Faria settled his civil rights lawsuit for $2 million, with no admission of wrongdoing.
Then, in July 2021, Lincoln County Prosecutor Mike Wood charged Pam Hupp with first-degree murder in Betsy Faria's death.
She pleaded not guilty.
Wood also opened an investigation into how the original case was handled.
In 2025, a former sheriff's captain on the case, Mike Merkel, was charged with perjury over his testimony in the Faria case. He is presumed innocent, and that case is pending.
The original prosecutor, Leah Askey, has denied any wrongdoing.
Hupp's trial has been moved and delayed again and again.
Her lawyers have pointed to DNA from an unidentified man on evidence, including the knife handle. Prosecutors dispute that it clears her.
In April 2026, Hupp waived her right to a jury, and the state dropped its pursuit of the death penalty.
A judge is scheduled to hear the case in January 2028.
Russ Faria spent about three and a half years locked up for a murder he was ultimately acquitted of.
Pam Hupp is serving life for killing Louis Gumpenberger. In Betsy's case, she is charged, not convicted, and presumed innocent.
Betsy Faria was 42 years old.
Nearly fifteen years after her death, no court has decided who killed her.
